paragraphs: Locating actions in video requires identifying both where an action occurs and when it happens. Training systems for this task usually requires manually drawing action boxes in every frame, which makes collecting training data expensive. This paper develops a framework that can learn from several kinds of annotation, including combinations of detailed and incomplete labels.

The model uses discriminative clustering and translates available supervision into constraints on its optimization. Those constraints can express a class label for an entire video, a marked time point, a small number of action boxes, or complete frame-by-frame boxes. This gives the different annotation types a shared role in training while preserving the information each provides.

Experiments on UCF101-24 and DALY report competitive detection performance using a fraction of the supervision required by previous methods. Adding a few fully annotated examples to weakly labeled videos also produces a significant improvement. The findings support collecting a mixture of annotation types as a useful way to train action localization systems.
neurips-2018-a-flexible-model-for-traini.tldr: A unified action-localization model combines sparse and detailed video annotations to achieve competitive results with substantially less supervision.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent may need to improve its performance while respecting constraints throughout training. This paper addresses that requirement using constrained Markov decision processes, where the main objective is accompanied by limits on expected cumulative costs. Safety is therefore expressed through these cost constraints, giving the learning problem a precise mathematical target.

The central contribution is a method for constructing Lyapunov functions that connect local decisions to the policy's overall safety. These functions produce local linear constraints that guarantee global safety of the behavior policy within the formulation. This connection makes an overall cost requirement actionable during learning, rather than leaving it only as a criterion for evaluating the final policy.

The authors use this foundation to turn dynamic programming and reinforcement learning algorithms into safe counterparts. Evaluations cover several planning and decision-making tasks in a safety benchmark domain. The proposed methods significantly outperform the tested baselines in balancing constraint satisfaction against performance, supporting the usefulness of the framework for learning under explicit cumulative-cost requirements.
neurips-2018-a-lyapunov-based-approach-t.tldr: Lyapunov functions translate cumulative safety requirements into local constraints for reinforcement learning and dynamic programming algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper examines how neural activity might represent uncertainty about the causes of sensory input. One debate asks whether responses encode individual samples or parameters of a probability distribution. Another asks whether activity relates directly to probabilities or to their logarithms. The authors show that these descriptions can be compatible within the same system.

Their central analytical result starts from a specific model: neural responses in visual area V1 are samples from a posterior over latent variables in a linear Gaussian model of images. Under that assumption, those responses also constitute a linear probabilistic population code. A sampling interpretation can therefore coexist with a population-level description of the represented distribution.

More specifically, the posterior over an experimenter-defined variable such as orientation belongs to the exponential family, with sufficient statistics that depend linearly on sampling-based firing rates. This explains how activity described as samples can also provide the quantities needed to describe a distribution. The result establishes compatibility under the stated model, rather than selecting a single universally correct account of neural coding.
neurips-2018-a-probabilistic-population-.tldr: Under a linear Gaussian image model, sampling-based neural responses also form a linear probabilistic population code.

paragraphs: This paper introduces collapsed compilation, an approximate inference method for discrete probabilistic graphical models. It combines sampling some variables with knowledge compilation for the remaining variables. The distinctive feature is that the method chooses which variable to sample next as computation proceeds, using the partially compiled representation already available.

This adaptive division of work helps exploit local structure and context-specific independence: relationships that simplify once particular variable values are known. Exact inference can naturally benefit from such structure, but approximate methods have difficulty using it. The partially compiled circuit also supplies an effective proposal distribution for importance sampling, helping guide the sampling component using information gathered during compilation.

The evaluation reports strong performance on standard benchmarks. When methods are given equal limits on the amount of exact inference, collapsed compilation is competitive with leading alternatives and surpasses them on several benchmarks. That comparison supports the value of coordinating compilation and sampling during execution, with the reported advantage applying to several tested cases rather than every benchmark.
neurips-2018-approximate-knowledge-compi.tldr: Collapsed compilation adaptively combines importance sampling and compiled inference to exploit structure in discrete probabilistic models.

paragraphs: Image features are commonly organized on a two-dimensional grid, but meaningful relationships can connect regions far apart in that grid. This paper learns a graph representation from image feature maps so that recognition can reason about relationships between regions. The graph becomes an additional representation through which information can move across the image.

Each graph vertex represents a learned cluster of pixels, while edges express similarity between clusters in feature space. The method learns how to propagate information across all vertices, allowing distant regions to influence one another. It can then project the resulting graph features back into a two-dimensional grid, connecting the graph computation to the representations used by existing networks.

The authors demonstrate end-to-end training and integration into existing architectures. They evaluate semantic segmentation, object detection, and object instance segmentation, reporting improvements over state-of-the-art methods in all three tasks. These results support the usefulness of learned regional relationships across several recognition settings, with long-range information exchange serving as a central motivation for the design.
neurips-2018-beyond-grids-learning-graph.tldr: Learned region graphs let image networks exchange information across distant regions and improve three visual recognition tasks.

paragraphs: Estimating a distribution over high-dimensional images depends heavily on a learning algorithm's inductive bias: the tendencies that guide what it learns from available examples. Successful image generation alone does not explain those tendencies. This paper develops an empirical framework for investigating how deep generative models generalize and what their learned distributions reveal about their bias.

The approach probes learning algorithms with carefully constructed training datasets. After training, the researchers measure properties of the resulting distribution and look for patterns in how the model generalizes. Designing the training evidence is central to the method: it provides a controlled way to investigate how what a model learns relates to the examples it receives.

The authors identify interesting generalization patterns and verify that they recur across the datasets, common models, and architectures examined. This consistency gives the observations significance beyond a single tested model configuration. The contribution is a systematic way to study generative learning behavior, together with empirical evidence of recurring patterns across the investigated settings.
neurips-2018-bias-and-generalization-in-.tldr: Carefully designed training datasets expose recurring patterns of bias and generalization in image-generating models.

paragraphs: Modeling a dynamical system requires summarizing its history in a form that retains what matters for predicting the future. Predictive State Representations offer spectral methods for discovering such summaries. Although these methods are consistent with unlimited data, their performance can be poor when observations are scarce. This paper uses imperfect domain knowledge to improve that situation.

The supplied knowledge takes the form of a proposed state representation that may contain useful information without being fully correct. The authors characterize theoretically when that representation is relevant and design spectral algorithms that exploit its relevant parts. Their method uses principal angles to identify those components and is robust to misspecification of the supplied representation.

Experiments include synthetic hidden Markov models, aircraft identification, and a gene splice dataset. Even weak domain knowledge can yield substantial improvements over standard predictive-state learning in these evaluations. The findings support treating an imperfect state description as useful side information: the algorithm can extract relevant structure while completing the representation through learning.
neurips-2018-completing-state-representa.tldr: A spectral learning method extracts useful parts of imperfect state descriptions to improve predictive state discovery with limited data.

paragraphs: This paper models sequences in which several count-valued quantities are observed over time. Its deep Poisson-gamma dynamical system learns multiple layers of hidden structure while capturing both immediate temporal dependencies and relationships extending further into the past. The aim is to represent hierarchical organization and temporal behavior together within a single probabilistic model.

The authors derive closed-form Gibbs sampling updates using data augmentation. Auxiliary hidden counts first propagate backward through time and upward through the hierarchy; latent variables are then sampled forward and downward. This arrangement supplies an inference procedure for the interacting layers and time steps. A stochastic gradient MCMC method further makes inference scalable to very long multivariate count sequences.

Experiments on synthetic and varied real-world data report excellent predictive performance. The learned layers also provide interpretable representations of how hierarchical and temporal information propagates. The findings therefore concern both prediction and understanding: the model produces useful forecasts while exposing structured hidden factors that organize the observed count data.
neurips-2018-deep-poisson-gamma-dynamica.tldr: Deep Poisson-gamma dynamical systems combine hierarchical structure and temporal dependencies to predict and interpret multivariate count sequences.

paragraphs: This paper develops the connection between planning under uncertainty and inference in probabilistic models. Its starting point is SOGBOFA, a heuristic planning algorithm previously shown to work well with large, factored state and action spaces. The authors analyze its computation to explain how a successful planning procedure can also be understood through an inference framework.

They show that SOGBOFA acts as a specialized inference algorithm combining a symbolic form of belief propagation with gradient ascent. This interpretation identifies the computational ingredients behind its solutions. It also provides a route for using the same style of symbolic computation in a different problem: Marginal MAP inference.

The second contribution is a reduction from Marginal MAP to maximum expected utility problems suited to SOGBOFA's symbolic machinery. This leads to AGS, an algebraic solver that uses gradients. Experiments illustrate its potential on difficult Marginal MAP problems. The paper thus contributes both an explanation of an existing planner and a new inference solver derived from that connection.
neurips-2018-from-stochastic-planning-to.tldr: An inference interpretation of SOGBOFA leads to a new algebraic gradient-based solver for Marginal MAP problems.

paragraphs: Graph matching is commonly formulated as a quadratic assignment problem. This paper broadens the mathematical functions available for representing the matching task. It introduces a large family called Separable Functions and studies how members of that family can connect the original discrete problem to optimization over continuous variables.

The authors show that these functions can approximate discrete graph matching asymptotically as approximation-control parameters vary. The asymptotic qualification matters: the result concerns behavior as those parameters change toward the relevant limit. They also investigate global optimality and develop extensions to Lawler's widely used quadratic assignment formulation that preserve convexity or concavity.

These theoretical results create opportunities for new graph-matching algorithms, and the paper makes that possibility concrete with solvers based on two particular Separable Functions. Evaluation on popular benchmarks verifies state-of-the-art performance for the proposed method. The contribution combines a broader formulation of graph matching with practical examples showing that this additional mathematical flexibility can support effective solvers.
neurips-2018-generalizing-graph-matching.tldr: A family of Separable Functions extends graph-matching formulations and yields solvers with state-of-the-art benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Novelty detection asks whether a new observation belongs to the familiar data distribution or is an outlier. This paper assumes that training examples describe only the inlier distribution. It develops an encoder-decoder approach that estimates how likely an observation is to have been generated by that distribution, giving the detection decision an explicitly probabilistic basis.

The main computational idea is to linearize the parameterized manifold representing the structure of inlier data. This local approximation makes the probability calculation feasible. The authors show how the probability factorizes and can be evaluated using local coordinates associated with the manifold's tangent space, connecting the learned representation to a calculable measure of inlier likelihood.

The paper also improves training of its autoencoder network. Together, the probability computation and training changes achieve state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets in the reported evaluation. These results support using the learned geometry of familiar data for probabilistic novelty detection under the assumption that training provides examples of inliers only.
neurips-2018-generative-probabilistic-no.tldr: A probabilistic autoencoder method uses local manifold geometry to estimate whether an observation comes from the learned inlier distribution.

paragraphs: Learned image compression maps pixels into a quantized latent representation and uses an entropy model to encode that representation into a bitstream. The entropy model describes the probabilities of the latent values, making its ability to capture their structure central to compression. This paper compares autoregressive, hierarchical, and combined probability models for that purpose.

The authors find that autoregressive and hierarchical priors capture complementary structure. Combining them improves compression beyond previous learned models, although autoregressive modeling can impose a substantial computational cost. The approach therefore involves a tradeoff between richer probability modeling and the computation required to use it.

The combined model reports state-of-the-art rate-distortion performance, with a 15.8% rate reduction over the hierarchical baseline. Reported savings relative to JPEG, JPEG2000, and BPG are 59.8%, 35%, and 8.4%, respectively. The authors also describe it, to their knowledge, as the first learned method to beat BPG on both PSNR and MS-SSIM. These findings indicate improved file-size and reconstruction-quality tradeoffs in the reported comparisons.
neurips-2018-joint-autoregressive-and-hi.tldr: Combining autoregressive and hierarchical entropy models improves learned image compression, with reported rate savings over BPG and other codecs.

paragraphs: A neural translation model uses an encoder and a decoder, each building hidden representations across multiple layers. This paper proposes coordinating those representations layer by layer as they progress from lower to higher levels. The goal is to make the two sides learn together at corresponding stages of their processing.

The method introduces layer-wise attention and mixed attention mechanisms to support this coordination. It also shares parameters between encoder and decoder layers, providing a way to regularize their learning and tie their representations together. These changes make cooperation between the two components an explicit part of the model's architecture and training.

When combined with the Transformer, layer-wise coordination improves results on three IWSLT and two WMT translation tasks. The reported scores are 34.43 BLEU for WMT16 English–Romanian and 29.01 BLEU for WMT14 English–German, both above the Transformer baseline. The findings support coordinating intermediate representations as a useful architectural change across the evaluated translation tasks.
neurips-2018-layer-wise-coordination-bet.tldr: Layer-wise attention and parameter sharing coordinate Transformer encoders and decoders, improving results on five translation tasks.

paragraphs: Tandem mass spectrometry produces spectra used to identify peptides, the protein subsequences present in a biological sample. This paper improves Didea, a dynamic Bayesian network algorithm that scores candidate peptides. Its central challenge is to expand how many parameters can be learned while retaining an optimization objective with reliable convergence properties.

The authors introduce Convex Virtual Emissions, a class of emission distributions that preserves concavity of Didea's conditional log-likelihood. These distributions generalize log-sum-exp and make maximum likelihood and conditional maximum likelihood estimation concave for a broad range of Bayesian networks. In Didea, they enable efficient learning of many parameters with global convergence; the previous framework could tune only one parameter through costly grid search.

The resulting scoring function substantially improves both scoring accuracy and downstream Fisher kernel analysis relative to the state of the art. Changes to the message-passing schedule also significantly improve runtime. The authors additionally connect the new concave score to related mass-spectrometry scoring functions, linking the expanded learning framework to existing approaches.
neurips-2018-learning-concave-conditiona.tldr: New emission distributions let Didea learn many peptide-scoring parameters with global convergence while improving accuracy and runtime.

paragraphs: Link prediction estimates whether two nodes in a network should be connected. Familiar heuristics, such as counting common neighbors, are simple and interpretable, but each builds in assumptions about what makes a connection likely. This paper investigates learning a suitable scoring rule from the network by examining the local structure around each candidate link.

The theoretical contribution is a framework for gamma-decaying heuristics. It brings a wide range of existing heuristics together and proves that those within the framework can be approximated well using local subgraphs. This result explains why a neighborhood around a candidate connection can retain substantial information about whether the connection exists.

Building on that analysis, the method extracts local subgraphs and uses a graph neural network to map their patterns to link existence. Its experiments report exceptionally strong performance and consistent results across a wide range of problems. The contribution combines a justification for local structural evidence with a learned predictor that can adapt its use of that evidence to the network.
neurips-2018-link-prediction-based-on-gr.tldr: A graph neural network learns link-prediction rules from local subgraphs, supported by theory showing they approximate many established heuristics.

paragraphs: Decision-making under uncertainty often involves maximizing reward while keeping a separate cost within a constraint. Constrained partially observable Markov decision processes express this combination. The paper addresses the difficulty of solving large instances when existing methods require an explicit environment model, a requirement that can make large real-world applications hard to handle.

The proposed algorithm, CC-POMCP, uses online Monte Carlo tree search and needs only a black-box simulator of the environment. It combines simulation-based search with optimization of parameters induced by a linear program. This supplies a way to address the reward objective and cost constraint within a planning method designed for large constrained problems.

In experiments, CC-POMCP converges to optimal stochastic action selection and scales to very large problems. The convergence statement is presented as an experimental finding. The results support the usefulness of combining simulator-based planning with cost constraints, extending the reach of constrained partially observable decision-making beyond methods that depend on an explicit model.
neurips-2018-monte-carlo-tree-search-for.tldr: CC-POMCP uses simulator-based tree search to handle large partially observable planning problems with reward objectives and cost constraints.

paragraphs: A reward that specifies the desired task may still make it difficult for an agent to learn useful behavior efficiently. This paper studies learning an additional intrinsic reward to assist that process. It follows the Optimal Rewards Framework, where the quality of an intrinsic reward is judged by the behavior it produces under the original, extrinsic task objective.

Earlier work in this framework learned rewards for planning agents based on lookahead search. The authors derive an algorithm for agents that themselves learn through policy gradients. The learned intrinsic rewards are added to the extrinsic rewards used by the policy learner, while their purpose remains improving performance on the task specified externally.

The evaluation augments an A2C learner for Atari games and a PPO learner for MuJoCo domains. Each is compared with the same policy-learning method using only extrinsic rewards. Performance improves in most tested domains, but not all. This supports the usefulness of learning auxiliary rewards for policy-gradient agents while preserving the finding that the benefits vary across domains.
neurips-2018-on-learning-intrinsic-rewar.tldr: Learned additive intrinsic rewards improve policy-gradient agents on most, but not all, tested Atari and MuJoCo domains.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions in linear contextual bandits under individual fairness requirements. Similar actions or individuals should receive approximately equal selection probabilities, even when maximizing reward would favor different treatment. The challenge is that the similarity measure defining fairness is unknown to the learner and must be understood through feedback.

The assumed measure is a Mahalanobis similarity metric. Feedback only identifies that a fairness violation occurred; it does not quantify how severe the violation was. This models a regulator who can recognize unfair treatment without providing a numerical definition of similarity. The learner must therefore improve its decisions using a relatively weak signal about the governing constraints.

The main result is an algorithm for adversarially chosen contexts whose number of fairness violations grows only logarithmically with the number of rounds T. At the same time, its regret relative to the best fair policy has the optimal order O(sqrt(T)). Under the stated assumptions, the algorithm therefore combines infrequent violations over time with strong reward performance against a fairness-respecting comparator.
neurips-2018-online-learning-with-an-unk.tldr: With violation-only feedback about an unknown Mahalanobis fairness metric, an online learner achieves logarithmically growing violations and optimal-order regret.

paragraphs: Deep neural networks often trail gradient boosting trees on tabular learning tasks. This paper explores whether assigning a separate regularization strength to each network weight can help the network make better use of relevant inputs. The obstacle is that this creates an enormous collection of hyperparameters, making ordinary tuning impractical.

Regularization Learning Networks address the tuning problem with an efficient scheme that minimizes a new Counterfactual Loss. The resulting models significantly improve on the tested neural networks and achieve performance comparable to gradient boosting trees. The strongest results come from an ensemble combining the two approaches.

The learned networks are extremely sparse, removing up to 99.8% of edges and 82% of input features. This sparsity also helps reveal which inputs the network considers important, making its use of the data easier to interpret. The authors further suggest that RLNs could efficiently handle tabular and unstructured inputs within one network, such as medical images accompanied by health records; this is presented as a possible application.
neurips-2018-regularization-learning-net.tldr: Learning a regularization strength for each weight produces sparse neural networks with tabular performance comparable to gradient boosting trees.

paragraphs: Normalization methods help train deep networks by controlling their activations. This paper introduces a loss term that encourages activation variance to remain stable across randomly sampled mini-batches. The quantity being controlled is the variation between batch-level variance estimates, making consistency of those estimates a direct training objective.

The authors prove that this regularizer encourages activations to concentrate around a few distinct modes. They also analyze a specific setting in which the inputs follow a mixture of two Gaussian distributions. Depending on the prior probabilities, the loss either brings the two groups together or separates them optimally in the sense of linear discriminant analysis.

The paper connects the proposed term to batch normalization, providing a regularization interpretation of that method. Experiments report higher accuracy than batch normalization for both convolutional and fully connected networks. Together, the analysis and experiments link a constraint on batch-to-batch variance fluctuations to the shape of learned activation distributions and to improved accuracy in the evaluated networks.
neurips-2018-regularizing-by-the-varianc.tldr: A loss that stabilizes activation variance across mini-batches encourages distinct modes and improves accuracy over batch normalization in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Training recurrent neural networks consumes substantial memory because hidden activations must be available during backpropagation. This paper investigates reversible hidden-state transitions, which allow earlier states to be reconstructed during the backward pass. Recomputing those states offers a way to reduce the activation storage that restricts which recurrent models can be trained.

The authors first establish a fundamental problem with completely storage-free reversal: a perfectly reversible recurrent network cannot forget information in its hidden state. They then introduce a scheme that stores a small number of bits, allowing forgetting while retaining exact reversal. This addresses the tension between recovering earlier states and letting the recurrent computation discard information.

The method achieves performance comparable to traditional models while reducing activation memory by a factor of 10–15. Applied to attention-based sequence-to-sequence models, it maintains performance with reductions of 5–10 times in the encoder and 10–15 times in the decoder. These figures concern activation memory, demonstrating substantial savings in that component of training.
neurips-2018-reversible-recurrent-neural.tldr: Storing a small amount of information lets reversible RNNs forget while reconstructing activations, substantially reducing training activation memory.

paragraphs: A policy can guide a search procedure toward promising actions, but the search algorithm determines how that guidance is used. This paper introduces two policy-guided tree search methods and gives guarantees on how many nodes they expand before finding goals. The methods target different patterns in the paths that lead to successful outcomes.

The first uses best-first enumeration with a cost function that supports an upper bound on node expansions before reaching a goal. It is particularly suited to needle-in-a-haystack problems. The second uses sampling and bounds the expected number of expansions before reaching a set of goals. It is better suited to cases where many paths can lead to success.

The authors evaluate both algorithms on 1,000 computer-generated Sokoban levels. A neural policy trained using A3C guides the search. The results are competitive with a state-of-the-art domain-independent heuristic planner. The contribution therefore combines practical policy-guided search with distinct guarantees that clarify how the two algorithms fit different goal-path structures.
neurips-2018-single-agent-policy-tree-se.tldr: Two policy-guided tree search algorithms bound search effort and suit different settings with rare or numerous paths to goals.

paragraphs: This paper uses differential equations to understand the dynamics of optimization algorithms through connections with physical systems. Its goal is to place several familiar methods within a common analytical framework. The physical viewpoint provides a way to study how an optimization process evolves, connecting algorithmic updates to the behavior of an associated dynamical system.

The framework covers gradient descent, proximal gradient descent, coordinate gradient methods, proximal coordinate gradient methods, and Newton's method. It also includes their Nesterov-accelerated variants. Bringing these methods together allows their dynamics to be studied using shared ideas, across algorithms that differ in which variables they update and which form of update they apply.

The analysis extends beyond problems assumed to be convex or strongly convex. In particular, it applies under Polyak–Łojasiewicz and error-bound conditions, which can include nonconvex problems. This broadens the mathematical settings available to the framework. The contribution is a unified perspective for analyzing optimization dynamics under these conditions, rather than a claim that arbitrary nonconvex problems are covered.
neurips-2018-the-physical-systems-behind.tldr: A differential-equation framework connects optimization algorithms to physical systems and applies under conditions that can extend beyond convexity.

paragraphs: Unsupervised image-to-image translation can struggle to change an individual object without also disturbing the background or relationships among objects. This paper addresses that difficulty by giving the translation system a learned attention mechanism. The motivation is to help the model identify the parts of a scene that are relevant to the desired transformation.

Attention is trained jointly with the generators and discriminators through adversarial learning. It therefore becomes part of the same learning process that produces and evaluates translated images. The approach requires no additional supervision for learning where to attend, allowing the focus of the transformation to emerge within the unsupervised setting.

The experiments show that the method can attend to relevant image regions and produce more realistic mappings than the recent approaches used for comparison. This supports the practical value of learning where a transformation should focus alongside learning the transformation itself. The evidence concerns observed improvements in attention and realism, with selective treatment of scene content motivating the model's design.
neurips-2018-unsupervised-attention-guid.tldr: Jointly trained unsupervised attention helps image translation focus on relevant regions and produce more realistic transformations.

paragraphs: This paper learns to recover an object's three-dimensional shape and camera pose from unlabeled images belonging to a particular object category. A convolutional network predicts both quantities from a single image. During training, several views of an object provide a consistency signal: the predicted shape, projected using predicted camera poses, should reproduce the observed views.

The shape is represented as a point cloud, and the authors develop a differentiable projection formulation so that reprojection error can train the model. This representation is intended to support efficient learning of detailed geometry. To address ambiguity in camera pose, they train an ensemble of pose predictors and then distill it into a single student predictor.

Experiments show that the distilled predictor estimates camera pose accurately, while the point-cloud representation supports detailed shape predictions. The approach brings shape and viewpoint estimation into a shared learning objective. Its supervision comes from agreement across the available views, connecting the image evidence used in training to the single-image predictions the network ultimately makes.
neurips-2018-unsupervised-learning-of-sh.tldr: Differentiable point-cloud projection and distilled pose predictors learn detailed 3D shape and camera pose from unlabeled multiview images.
